ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Targeted Road Building Plans 
*101.    SHRI SURESH KALMADI †: 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
Will the Minister of ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have any plan to take up targeted road building 
in various parts of the country during the next financial year, particularly, in view 
of the wide-spread damage caused to roads and bridges in Gujarat due to recent 
earthquake; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, including cost of the proposed road building in 
various States and the participation of the State Governments, in their respective areas; 
(c) whether any foreign assistance is available for implementing these 
plans; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OFTHE MINISTRY OF ROAD TRANSPORT 
AND HIGHWAYS (MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI): (a) to (d)Astatement 
is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. National Highway Development Project (NHDP) comprising of 
Golden Quadrilateral and North-South and East-West Corridors  
† Thc question was actually askew on the floor of the house by Shri Suresh Kalmadi. 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2001] 
taken up by the Government will continue in the next financial year. 
In addition, improvement works on National Highways other than 
NHDP are also proposed to be taken up in various States. Immediate 
repairs to damages caused to roads and bridges in Gujarat during 
recent earthquake have already been carried out. 
(b) Four laning of 2027 Kms. of National Highways at an estimated cost 
of about Rs. 11,000.00 crore under NHDP are scheduled to be awarded 
by June 2001. In addition, improvement works amounting to 
Rs. 3028.76 crore are included in the proposed Annual Plan 2001-02 
for National Highway Sections other than NHDP in various States. 
Development of National Highways is fully financed by the Central 
Government. Involvement of State Government is by way of being 
the implementing agencies for National Highways for non NHDP 
Sections. 
(c) and (d) Apart from on-going projects financed by them, World Bank 
and Asian Development Bank have shown interest in providing loan 
assistance for financing part of the NHDP during the next financial 
year also. Details in this regard have not yet been finalised by them. 
SHRI SURESH KALMADI: Mr. Chairm an, Sir, many ambitious road 
projects have been announced which, by itself, is a good thing. But the 
implementation of the same has been very tardy. A provision of Rs. 2500 crores 
has been made under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana for rural roads, 
But I believe not a pie out of it has been spent this year. Under the ambitious 
programme of Golden Quadrilateral only 600 Kms. have been covered so far. 
Why is the delay? Are the bureaucratic controls still very, very strong that it 
could not happen? Even the Planning Commission has criticised the 
Government for taking up the highway development projects without proper 
planning. You had to put a cess on petrol and diesel; collecting about Rs. 6000 
crores. In about seven to eight years you will be collecting Rs. 60,000 crores. 
But the total amount required is much, much more for die improvement of 
roads. Therefore, is there any plan to involve the private sector? In your reply, 
you have said that you are talking to the Asian Development, World Bank, etc. 
Have you any plans to involve the private sector in the road building activity? 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI: Mr. Chairman, Sir, as I understand, 
the hon. Member has raised three questions. The first is pertaining to the rural 
roads. I would like to clarify that this subject is being dealt with by the Ministry 
2 

[1 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
of Rural Development; not by the Ministry of Surface Transport. A provision of 
Rs. 2500 crores-has been made. At this stage, it is not proper to say that nothing 
has been done. The House may recollect, the Road Bill has been passed by bom 
the Houses only in the Winter Session, i.e., last December. The money has 
already been allotted. But list containing the details of the roads have to come 
from the State Governments to the Central Government Then, the Central 
Government would give its approval. Therefore, it is not fair to say in regard to the 
scheme which has just commenced in December—that nothing is on the 
ground. The State Governments have to give certain feedback. I am sure this will 
be in place very soon. 
SHRI SURESH KALMADI: You have made a provision of Rs. 2500 crores 
for this year, but nothing has been spent. That is what I had said. 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI: This whole process was approved 
by Parliament only in the month of December. The scheme was announced on 
the 25th December. Therefore, I think we should give a little time for things to get 
going. 
The second thing the hon. Member talked about is the Golden Quadrangle 
and its tardy implementation. I would like to humbly submit that this is not a fair 
assessment. The scheme which has been started is indeed a very ambitious 
scheme. For the first time in thecountry, in 50 years of independence, such a 
scheme has been mooted. About 5,952 Kms. of the Golden Quadrangle is 
planned to be connected. I would like to inform the hon. Member that the 
whole thing is going on very much on schedule and in a very organised manner. 
I would only like to give one or two instances. After having conceived this 
scheme, initially, a lot of ground work had to be done. Such a scheme has never 
been tiiought of earlier, leave alone its implementation. Actually, the Golden 
Quadrangle alone is scheduled to be completed in 2004. After going into the 
details, we have organised everything. We have preponed it to December, 2003. 
Therefore, to say that the progress of this project is tardy is not correct At the 
moment; if things are not in place it is because it takes time. Now, about 1200 
Kms. of roads have to be completed by June. About 5,952 Kms. would have to be 
completed sometime by-the middle of next year. Therefore, this project will be 
completed as per schedule. The work is  going on as per schedule. Things are 
totally under control. I can assure the Housej-there is nothing to worry about. 
The third thing you have asked is about the role of private sector. We are very 
much wanting the private sector, to take part in our schemes. In the funding 
pattern, we have very much taken cognizance of the private sector. The private 
3 

RAJYA SABHA            [1  March, 2001 ] 
sector is coming in at the moment. We have got over Rs. 1000 crores worth of 
Build, Operate andTransfer, BOT, projects. We have 20 of them. Eleven of them 
have been completed and the rest are ongoing. Further we are going in even for 
Govemrnent-to-Govemrnent projects. With Malaysia, we have signed an MoU 
for Rs. 760 crores. The final agreemen t will soon be cleared. Another 600 
kilometres of the Calcutta Vivekananda Bridge is also to come up soon. For 
another 600-700 kilometres, the Malaysian Government is coming in. The 
Indian private sector as well as other private sectors are very much part of our 
projects. We have given a lot of facilities. For some of them, that is, the Build, 
Operate, Transfer, Projects, grant up to 40 per cent has been permitted. We have 
given the private sector income-tax concession for five years. Yesterday, it has 
been announced that it would be 10 years, On the total income-tax, 30 per cent 
concession has been given for the next 20 years. They can pick up any 10 years 
out of those 20 years We have made model concession agreements for the 
private sector. The private sector is coming in. Apart from BOT, we have also 
gone in for Annuity payments. There was some problem with regard to the toll 
collection. They have got some reservation there. Therefore, we very much 
want the private sector to come in. We are making the maximum use of them. 
SHRI SURESH KALMADI: Would the Prime Minister think in terms of 
bringing both the Gramin Sadak Yojana and the Golden Quadrilateral project under 
one Ministry? Now they are under two different Ministries. These sort of projects, 
the integration of National Highways, State Highways and the roads, must all be 
an integrated plan. If you have two Ministries, the left hand might not know what 
the right hand is doing. So, there should be one particular Ministry. Would the 
Prime Minister think in terms of one Ministry for them? This sort of a big project, 
one would assume, would be employment-oriented. A lot of people should get 
work in this big, Rs. 60,000-crore, project. The national re-construction of roads 
should be a big employment factor. But, unfortunately, it is bringing in only foreign 
companies. In the tender forms, there is priority for people who bring in modem 
equipment whereas we have got a vast manpower which can be used for this road-
building exercise. Most of your contracts are going to foreign companies and the 
Indian companies which are quite big are given only sub-contracts. I think this not 
in the scheme of things. So, would you think of making this employment-oriented? 
The Indian companies should get priority in this so that only bringing in the latest 
equipment from abroad may not be the criterion. 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI: On the question about one Ministry, 
it is not appropriate for me to reply. But let me humbly suggest that it is not 
4 

[1 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
right to say that the left hand does not know what the right hand is doing. I can 
give you the total picture of the cess money being used, what the Rural Ministry 
is using. But, concept-wise, rural development is a separate Ministry. You have 
talked about the Gram in Sadak Yojana. Appropriately, that should be dealt with 
by the Rural Development Ministry. And the Planning Commission is coordinating 
it. There is no difficulty. If more details are required, I would also be in a position 
to give them as to what is happening. 
As regards the total concept of roads, let me inform the House that India 
has got 33 lakh kilometres of road. Out of that only 57,737 kilometres is National 
Highways, which my Ministry is supposed to look after; 1,28,000 kilometres is 
State Highways; 4,70,000 kilometres are major district roads which are being 
looked after by the States. 26.5 lakh k ilometres are the gramin, village roads. 
The last three are looked after by the States as far as maintenance is concerned. 
The Golden Quadrilateral which is coming up now and the development of the 
National Highways; as many as 13,300 kilometres are looked after by our Ministry. 
Even for the States, the cess money is going. This year, we have given to the 
States Rs. 990 crores for the city roads and major district roads. The concept of 
the Prime Minister is that the roads in totality, 33 lakh kilometres, in India should 
be looked at and improved upon and the National Highways should be raised to 
international standards. That is the concept, and that is why this division has 
been done. The third point which the hon. Member has raised is that it is not 
employment oriented, and a lot of foreign companies are being given the contracts. 
This is not factually correct. First of all, we very much wanted it to be employment 
oriented. But, we have to keep in mind that for better quality of roads, the 
modem techniques have to be used and per force, we have to depend on better 
machines. To the extent the roads can be made of a good quality, the manpower 
would be employed. As regards the aspect of foreign companies, there is some 
misconception. Factually, as of last week, there were 54 contracts which have 
been given by the National Highways Development Programme. Out of 54 
contracts, 37 have been given to Indian companies, 11 contracts have been 
given to joint ventures—Indian and foreign—and only six companies out of the 
whole lot of 54 companies are foreign. Therefore, we have a total transparent 
system of tendering. We have got a pre-qualification arrangement that is 
necessary in order to ensure that only those people who are qualified, come 
forward. The Government is giving a tremendous amount of assistance for this 
purpose. Our own people have been permitted to import custom-free road building 
machinery which is not being produced in India. So, all this is being done with a 
view to ensuring that we employ our own internal indigenous capability to a 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [ 1 March, 2001] 
greater extent But the areas where it is not possible or where something better or 
cheaper is being available, we are making use of that. 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Sir, I must congratulate the Minister for his 
very pious intentions. Some time ago, I think, almost a year ago, the hon. Prime 
Minister had announced the National Express Highway, connecting the North 
and the South. But from all the information available to us as citizens, it has not 
yet taken off, and the blue print is only on the paper. I would like to know from 
the hon. Minister one thing. Is it one of the reasons that the said highway 
project is not taking off at all due to compensation to be paid to those people 
whose land has to be acquired? If that is so, wasn't this taken into consideration 
when the highway project was announced? Similarly, yesterday's Budget puts a 
lot of responsibility on the State Governments by giving them the cess amounting 
to Rs. 1,000 crores for the State roads. Would there be any monitoring agency to 
ensure that this money is spent on roads which are badly needed in different 
States or would this money be diverted for some other purpose? What steps is 
the Government taking to pay adequate compensation to those people, especially, 
in the agricultural sector, would be losing their land for this purpose? 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI: Sir, the North-South and East-
West Corridor consists of 7300 Kms. of road. As of now, it starts from Silcher to 
Porbunder and from Srinagar in Jammu and Kashmir to Kanyakumari. It is not 
correct to say that this is being delayed or there has been a delay in our planning. 
This is to be completed by 2007. The Golden Quadrilateral is to be completed by 
2003. Therefore our emphasis, while awarding the contracts is also on the Golden 
Quadrilateral. Although, about 400 kms. of road North-South and East-West 
Corridor has already been completed, we are going to concentrate on this after 
we have finished awarding by June th is year for the Golden Quadrilateral. 
Thereafter, there will be total concen tration on North-South and East-West 
Corridors, and this will also go as per schedule. I hope it to be completed before 
2007, but certainly, there is no problem in planning or in implementing the same. 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: I am talking of the acquisition of the land. 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI: I am coming to that point The 
question of land acquisition has always been a problem, particularly, in some of 
the States, where there is shortage of la nd, where the land is very costly. For 
instance, this has been a problem in Kerala. Therefore, at the Government of 
India's level, we have revised the system of land acquisition, and now, as per the 
present system which has been introduced recently, we have authorised a State 
6 

[ 1 March, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
Government person by name. Normally, it is the District Magistrate. He is being 
authorised by me to go ahead and carry out the land acquisition. How much 
money is to be paid as compensation for acquiring the land, is all fixed by the 
State Government. They do ail this work for us and we make the payment. 
There has been some problem in some areas. But with this new system, the State 
Governments are also participating very positively in this, and the land 
acquisition problem has been reduced considerably. Ther e are some areas; 
mere are some cases. We certainly have to lay emphasis on this. I have written 
to the Chief Ministers requesting them to lay a little more emphasis on this. But 
the system has been simplified and we hope that this will not be a major problem. 
In some places some problems will be there. But this will not be a major problem. 
As regards the third point of monitoring the States, we are very much 
aware of it. I have told you that an amount of Rs. 990 crores is allotted for both 
rural and State roads. The system that we have evolved is this. We have released 
the first lot, that is one-third of this Rs. 990 crores, in the month of November 
itself. On that basis, the Ordinance has been issued. The money has gone to the 
States. The States have forwarded the list of roads which they want to develop 
and they have sent us the rough estimates. They are getting checked by my 
Ministry. If we are satisfied that it is being utilised properly, we clear it. The 
States will utilise that one-third and thereafter give us their requirement. In fact, 
we are giving them sanction for the full amount of money that has been allotted 
to them so that there is no delay. But the payment will depend on the physical 
utilisation of that money on those roads that have already been sanctioned and 
not anywhere else, even on other road s. Thereafter, monitoring has been 
effectively done.

PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY: Sir, like any other infrastructure, for 
roads not only construction but also maintenance is equally important. What steps 
does the Government propose to take for the maintenance of roads that have 
already been constructed? How much money has the Government allotted for this 
purpose? What is the porcess of monitoring? This is part (a) of my question. Part 
(b) of my question is this. I have heard that the private sector is unwilling to 
invest in this capital-intensive sector. The hon. Minister has mentioned that 
much impetus has been given to the private sector. What is the input so far the last 
year or the year before the last? There is a fear in the road sector, a genuine 
concern among them that the major co ntracts would be cornered by the 
multinational companies with the Indian companies becoming merely 
subcontractors. What steps does the Government plan to take for protecting the 
interest of the Indian companies? 
MA J. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI: Sir, the first part of the question of 
Hon'ble Member was about the mainte nance arrangement and the monitoring 
system. Sir, it is a very important aspect which is constantly attracting our 
attention. At the moment, we are trying to bring these roads, particularly the 
National Highways of 57,737 kilometres up to a certain standard. We are 
doing it in two ways. Firstly, the National Highways Authority of India is doing 
the NHD programme. They will take up 14,000 kilometres of road and convert 
that into four-lane or six-lane. Theref ore, these roads will be completed and 
brought to a certain stan dard. Thereafter, the methodology that we adopt is 
this; these roads are maintained by the NHAI through a toll system. They 
collect the toll and plough back that money into maintenance of roads. Now 
in regard to the roads which have .been given on BOT arrangement, the 
concession agreement varies from 15 years to 30 years. That means for that 
period these agencies will have to maintain those roads up to the required 
standards. This arrangement will enable  us to keep the roads going, at least 
these 14,000 kilometres of roads which are, at the moment, under the NHDP. 
The rest of the roads are to be maintained directly by my Ministry. We have got 
an organisation. This maintenance work is being done through the State PWDs. 
This needs to be understood. Generally, it is not known. We are giving money 
to the State PWDs as maintenance agencies. We do not have a separate 
maintenance agency at the Central level. In the reply, 1 have stated that we 
have now made a provision of Rs. 3028.76 crores in the coming year for this 
purpose. There are various activities which have to be done. At the moment, 
for improving the roads there is a programme called NHO. In this, the first 
thing is widening of roads and making pavements. The 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [ 1 March, 2001 ] 
second thing is improving the riding quality (IRQP) and the third thing is repair 
and maintenance. We have to do all these things. But for that we need a very large 
quantum of money. As of today, if I want to bring these 57,000 kilometres up to a 
certain level, I need Rs. 1,65,000 crores. This much money is not available with us. 
Therefore, we are trying to do in it in stages, slowly and gradually. We are first 
trying to bring these two-lane roads up to a certain standard. Thereafter, as and 
when, we complete these 13,000 kilometres which come under NHDP, hopefully, 
other roads will also will be converted into four-lane or six-lane. This is the 
system. We will do that. The last part of the supplementary was a bout 
multinationals. I have got the figures. This information that the multinationals are 
cornering the contracts is not correct. We will not allow them to do it. We are 
engaging our own people. I have given you many examples about how we are 
doing it, including allowing our people to import very costly machine. A number 
of people have imported them. We have allowed free imports. We have also given 
them tax incentives. As regards the number of people, out of 54, only six are 
outsiders. I am sure that such a thing will not happen, and we will have a check 
on it. Our own people must come forward. That is why we also, sometimes, 
reduce the package. Ideally speaking, we should have done 100 kms. in one 
contract. But we are reducing it so that people with low financial capability can 
also come in.

Kerala Package 
*103. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Kerala package announced by the Prime Minister during his visit 
to Kerala especially for the agriculture sector was termed as a farce; 
(b) whether it is a fact that no Government decision has been taken on any of 
the programmes announced and the State Government has so far not received any 
information on the package; 
(c) if so, what are the facts; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to make the package operational? 
THE MINISTER OFAGRICUTLURE (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) to (d) The 
accouncements made by the Prime Minister at Kumarakom in Kerala on 31.12.2000 
covered several issues besides agriculture, such as aviation, ports, railways, 
tourism, information technology and higher education. These issues have been 
taken up with the concerned Administrative Ministries for their implementation. As 
far as Ministry of Agriculture is concerned, Prime Minister announced: 
(i) More procurement of copra at a higher support price from this season in 
coordination with the State Government depending upon the 
storage facility; 
(ii) Setting up of a Technology Mission for Coconut covering areas like 
cultivation, protection against pests and plant diseases, 
diversification, value addition, storage and marketing facilities. 
With regard to procurement of copra, the report of the Commission for 
Agriculture Costs and Prices on copra price policy for 2001 season is under 
consideraiton of the Government. The Minimum Support Price (MSP) for 2001 
season will be announced shortly. The interest of growers will be kept in mind 
while fixing the MSP. Meanwhile, over 2 lakh MT of copra have already been 
procured by NAFED at the existing rate.

New Year Eve Musing on Kashmir 
*106. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Pakistan Foreign Minister gave a welcome response to the 
Prime Minister's New Year Eve musing on Kashmir, indicating an expectation for 
a purposeful dialogue between India and Pakistan; 
(b) if so, the details of the Prime Minister's observations referred to as New 
Year Eve musing on Kashmir and Pakistan's response thereto; and 
(c) the details of the ensuing dialogue? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFA1HS (SHRI JAS WANT SINGH): (a) 
to (c) In his article titled "Kumarakom Musings" appearing in January 2001 Prime 
Minister, Atal Bihari Vajpayee, wrote, "The Kashmir problem is an unfortunate 
inheritance from the tragic partition of India in 1947. India never accepted the 
pernicious Two-Nation theory that brought about the partition. However, the 
mindset that created Pakistan continues to operate in that country. This is why it is 
continuing with its untenable po licy on Kashmir, disregarding the 
considerations of both good neighbourly relations with India and the well being of 
the people of Jammu and Kashmir. 
India is willing and ready to seek a lasting solution to the Kashmir problem. 
Towards this end, we are prepared to recommence talks with Pakistan at any 
level, including the highest level, provided Islamabad gives sufficient proof of 
its preparedness to create a conducive atmosphere for a meaningful dialogue. 1 
am sad to note, however, that the Government of Pakistan is not doing enough to 
rein-in terrorist organizations based on its soil that are continuing their killing 
spree, targeting both innocent civilians and our security personnel in Kashmir 
and other parts of India". 
He also wrote, "In our search for a lasting solution to the Kashmir problem, both 
in its external and internal dimensioins, we shall not traverse solely on the beaten 
track of the past. Rather, we shall be bold and innovative designers of a future a 
architecture of peace and prosperity for the entire South Asian region. In this search, 
the sole light that will guide us is our commitment to peace, justice and the vital 
interests of the nation." 
There has been no formal statment from Pakistan. However, several 
comments attributed to Pakistani leaders have appeared in the Pakistani Press on 
the Prime Minister's article. In one such report, Foreign Minister of Pakistan 
28 

[ 1 March, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
was quoted as having said, "We have taken due note of the statement that has been 
made specially by India and Indian Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee on the 
New Year eve... we are impressed by wh at Indian Prime Mi nister has said." 
Notwithstanding such comments, there is no evidence of any change in Pakistan's 
sponsorship of cross border terrorism in the State of Jammu and Kashmir or 
elsewhere in India. Pakistan continues to give state patronage to obscurantist 
groups indulging in violence beyond its borders. 
India desires the establishment of good neighbourly relations with 
Pakistan. We have reiterated our commitment to resuming the Composite 
Dialogue, so as to build trust and confid ence, establish a stable structure of 
cooperation and address outstanding is sues. For this, self evidently, an 
appropriate atmosphere is needed. That  is why we expect from Pakistan an 
abjurement of violence; ceasing promotion, encouragement and abetment of cross 
border terrorism; and a commitment to the Simla Agreement of 1972 and 
Lahore Declaration of 1999.

Viability of SSI Units 
*108. SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIESANDAGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the details of the existing credit guarantee and banking services extended 
by Government for the development of small scale sector industrial units; 
(b) whether Government propose to consider to enhance the same for 
increasing the financial viability of the units; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether there is any specific propo sal to ensure protection against 
dumping of products in the small scale units; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI 
VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) to (c) The Government has launched a Credit 
Guarantee Fund Scheme with a view to alleviating the problem of collateral 
security and impediment to flow of credit to Small Scale Industries sector. 
This scheme is being operated by the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small 
Industries (CGTSI) through member lending institutions i.e. scheduled 
commercial banks (either Public Sector Undertaking, Private or Foreign Banks), 
select Regional Rural Banks, National Small Industries Corporation or any 
other institutions as may be directed by the Government. This scheme provides 
guamtee cover upto 75% of credit (term loan and working capital loan) to 
30 

[1 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
new and existing Small Scale Units on loans upto Rs. 25 lakhs. The rate of 
interest under the scheme can not exceed 3% above the prime lending rate of 
Prime Lending Institutions. As regards banking services, Government of India 
has taken various policy measures for increasing the flow of credit to the small 
scale units which inter-alia includes earmarking 60% of the SSI credit under 
priority sector lending for the tiny sector, dispensing with collaterals for loans 
upto Rs. 5 lakhs, formulation of Credit Guarantee Scheme, enhancement of 
Composite Loan limit to Rs. 25 lakhs, enhancement of limit of project cost 
upto Rs. 50 lakhs under the National Equity Fund Scheme, opening up of 
specialised SSI bank branches and simplified procedure for sanction of working 
capital loan upto Rs.5 crores based on normative requirement of 20% of the 
annual projected turnover of the units, to delegate adequate powers to the 
managers of specialised small scale industries branches with a.view to avoiding 
delay in disposal of loan application etc. All these meas ures are likely to 
enhance the financial viability of the SSI sector. 
(d) and (e) In order to provide protection against dumping of products, 
the Government has set up the Directorate General of Anti-Dumping & Allied 
Duties in the Department of Commerce under the control of Designated 
Authority. According to the Anti-Dumping Rules, initiation of Anti-Dumping 
investigation is undertaken when the domestic industry files a fully documented 
petition to the Designated Authority with prima-facie evidence of dumping, 
injury and casual link between the dumping of the imported goods and injury 
to domestic industry. The Designated Authority may also initiate investigations 
suo-mofo, if it is satisfied with the information received from the Collector of 
Customs or from any other source that sufficient evidence exists regarding 
dumping of the foreign goods, material injury to the domestic industry and 
casual link between the two. Based on  the information received by the 
Government concerning unfair trade pr actices leading to imports of cheap 
consumer goods like Dry Batteries, Sports Shoes and Toys from China causing 
injury to the domestic industry, the Directorate General of Anti-Dumping & 
Allied Duties initiated suo-moto investigations against the import of Dry 
Batteries, Sports Shoes and Toys from China on 20.11.2000. Provisional duty 
has been recommended on Dry Batteries on 24.1.2001 and on Sports Shoes on 
25.1.2001. The case of toys has been closed since there was no sufficient 
evidence of injury to justify the continuation of investigations.

† *109. SHRIRAMJETHMALANI: 
DR. D. MASTHAN: 
Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND 
RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any assessment has been made by Government regarding the 
impact on the small scale industries of the country after removing all restrictions 
on imports in the coming months; 
(b) whether it is a fact that a number of institutions engaged in compilation 
of statistics in the country have pointed out the difficulties coming before the 
small scale industries; and 
(c) if so, the details of such difficulties and what decision has been taken 
by Government to safeguard the small scale industries from such difficulties? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI 
VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) to (c) Government is constantly monitoring the impact 
of the removal of Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) on the economy including the 
SSI sector. Historically, there have been some difficulties which have been faced 
by this sector which include inter-alia, availability of timely credit, 
technological obsolescence, labour legi slations, infrastructure! difficulties, 
managerial problems, etc., which have not been accentuated by the removal of 
QRs. 
A number of institutions including the SSI Associations, etc., have pointed 
out that the removal of the QRs have exposed the SSIs to greater competition. 
The Government has put in place several measures to help them become globally 
competitive. A new SSI policy was announced during the National Conference 
on SSI held at New Delhi during 30-31 August, 2000, Some of the major 
incentives/measures include raising the excise exemption limit from Rs. SO 
lakhs to Rs. 1 crore, a scheme of Capital Subsidy of 12% for investment in 
technology upgradation in select sectors, raising the eligibility limit for coverage 
under the Credit Guarantee Scheme from Rs. 10 lakhs to 25 lakhs, continuation 
of financial support to SSI units for ob taining ISO 9000 certification, for the 
next 6 years, etc. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
32 

[1 March,200I] RAJYASABHA 
Even after the removal of Quantitative Restrictions (QRs), protection to 
the industries is available in the form of raising Custom Duties upto the bound 
levels, imposing Anti-Dumping duties and countervailing duties, taking 
safeguard measures, in case of surge in imports, etc. On the other hand, with the 
lowering of tariffs and the removal of QRs, the SSI units will be able to get raw 
material and other inputs without the hassles of Import Licences and at 
competitive prices. Further, the opening of markets by other countries, and 
lowering of their tariffs will provide an opportunity to SSI units to give a big 
boost to their exports. 
Government is fully aware of the WTO environment and is taking 
appropriate measures for preparing the Small Scale Sector to meet the challenges 
of liberalisation and globalisation.

706. SHRI CO. POULOSE: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any study on the danger of import of fish, 
which is likely to destroy the fish industry in the country and thus it Would displace 
10 million fishermen;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(DR. DEBENDRA PRADHAN): (a) to (c) Wh ile no specific study has been 
made, an analysis of the data on import offish into the country indicates that 
during the last three years, quantities ranging between 5,000-11,000 tonnes 
offish have been imported annually which constitute 0.09% to 0.21% of the total

sample checks in 25 States and 6 UTs and an all India survey to assess the 
beneficiary perception of the PDS conducted by ORG-MARG Research limited. 
The estimates of diversion have been quoted from a study report by TECS 
which was commissioned by the Ministry of Food, ConsumerAffairs and Public 
Distribution in 1997. 
The.State Governments have been requested to closely monitor the PDS 
at the Fair Price Shop (FPS) and othe r levels and to make arrangement for 
distribution of PDS commodities in a transparent and accountable manner by 
involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs). Involvement of Panchayati 
Raj Institution in the implementation of TPDS as a measure of social audit will 
make the system more transparent an d accountable and thereby helping in 
checking the diversion of food item under PDS to a large extent. They have 
also been asked to eliminate bogus ration cards and initiate action against 
ejring FPS owners under section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. 
Extracts of the CAG's report are being forwarded to the State Governments 
and UT Administrations concerned for taking remedial steps.

744. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRA1AH: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to

(a) whether Government have been urged to ensure payment of reasonable 
price to sugarcane growers by sugar mills; 
(b) if so, whether a number of sugar mills had been closed in various parts 
of the country; 
(c) if so, whether Government's intervention was required to help the cane 
growers; 
(d) whether the cane growers in Karnataka, Bihar, Maharashtra and Andhra 
Pradesh are in great threat due to non-payment of dues by the sugar mills; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): 
(a) The Statutory Minimum Price (SMP) of sugaracane is fixed by the 
Central Government for each sugar seas on taking into acco unt the cost of 
production of sugarcane, return to the grower from the alternative crops and the 
general trend of price of agricultural commodities, availability to the consumer 
at a fair price, the price at which sugar produced from sugarcane is sold by the 
producers of sugar, the recovery of sugar from sugarcane etc. The SMP has been 
increased every season. However, most of the mills pay either the State Advised 
Price of sugarcane or agreed price which is much higher than the SMP. 
(b) A statment showing the State-wise details of sugar mills which have 
remained continuously closed during the last three sugar seasons (October— 
September) is attached (Sec Below). 
The closure of sugar mills is attributable to variety of factors such as 
inadequate cane availability, uneconomic size, old age, bad condition of plant 
and machinery, technical and manageri al incompetence, excessive high cane 
price not commensurate with the sales realisation of sugar etc. 
(c) The Central Government has been providing financial assistance to 
the sugar mills from Sugar Development Fund (SDF) under different schemes 
viz. modernisation/rehabilitation and cane development. Till 31.12.2000, a

BPL and APL families 
† 747. PROF. M.M AGARWAL: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have defined the persons "living Below Poverty 
Line" and those "living Above Poverty Line"; 
(b) if so, the criterion adopted by Government for defining these categories; 
(c) whether Government have since decided not to give ration and sugar to 
those who are living above the poverty line; 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(e) Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF CONSUMERAFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIAM CHAUHAN): (a)and(b) 
Based on the recommendations of the Expert Group on Estimation of Proportion 
and Number of Poor (Lakdawala Committee) the Government has applied state-
specific poverty estimates in order to identify the poor i.e., persons living below the 
poverty line (BPL). These State-wise poverty estimates have been worked out by the 
Planning Commission from the national level poverty lines, using state-specific 
price indices and inter-state price diffe rentials. The national poverty lines are 
expressed as monthly per capita consumption expenditure of Rs. 49.09 in rural 
areas and Rs. 56.64 in urban areas at 1973-74 prices corresponding to a basket 
of goods and services anchored on a norm of per capita daily calorie 
requirement of 2400 kcal in rural areas and 2100 kcal in urban areas. 
(c) to (e) With a view to restructuring of Public Distribution System (PDS) for 
levy sugar, the Govt, has decided that w.e.f. 1.2.2001, levy sugar supply under 
PDS will be restricted to only BPL families except in case of North-Eastem 
States, Hilly States and Island Territories. The Govt, has also decided to allocate 
sugar under PDS on the basis of projected population as on 1.3.2000 and the 
per capita norm for allocation of sugar has also been enhanced from 425 gms. 
to 500 gms. per month.

allocation of wheat and rice is not demand based. Government of India has increased the

Second round Indo-China security dialogue 
760.     SHRJABAN1ROY: 
SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India and China held the second round of security dialogue 
recently in New Delhi as reported in the Indian Express dated 9th February, 2001; 
(b) what are the details of the talks and outcome thereof indicating whether 
Beijing's Nuclear and missile assistance to Pakistan and the question of Kashmir 
were also figured in the dialogue; and 
(c) if so, what are the issues on wh ich both sides share a similarity of 
approach including international security (NMD) and the other issue where 
both sides differed with each other? 
* 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI AJIT KUMAR PANJA): (a) to (c)The second round of India-China security 
dialogue was held in New Delhi on February 8, 2001. Both sides underlined 
that the aim of the dialogue is to enhance mutual understanding, expand common 
ground in approach to international and regional security affairs and narrow 
down differences. They held common views on a number of contemporary, 
regional and international issues such as the desirability of a genuine poly-centric 
and equitable world order, concern about effects of globalisation on the economies 
of developing countries and the lasting validity of the principles of 
108 

[ 1 March, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
Panchsheel. China expressed concerns about some of the impending 
developments in the field of international security and their likely impact on 
global strategic stability. India views exploitation of outer space solely for 
the sake of socio-economic development of its people and looks forward to 
international cooperation to this end. Th erefore, India is for prevention of an 
arms race in outer space. During the talks, India's concerns were conveyed to 
China on the issue of lattcr's nuclear  and missile assistance to Pakistan. 
Chinese side reiterated that its cooper ation with Pakistan on nuclear and 
missile technology conformed to existing international regime on non-
proliferation. The Chinese delegation was also apprised of India's peace 
initiatives in Jammu & Kashmir, notwithstanding continued terrorist violence 
supported from across the border. The Chinese side stated that it was 
completely opposed to all forms of terrorism. China did not wish to mediate 
between India and Pakistan, and favoured a resumption of dialogue between 
India and Pakistan.

(SHRI AJIT KUMAR PANJA): (a) Yes, Sir. India-Nepal Foreign Secretary Level

(b) and (c) The two sides reviewed the progress in implementing the 
understandings reached during the visit of the Prime Minister of Nepal to India 
in July/August, 2000 and agreed to expedite pending issues. In this context, it

between the two countries would be utilised fully in order to achieve quicker 
progress on issues under discussion. 
109 

RAJYASABHA [1 March,200l] 
The two sides reiterated their determination to expand the diversify their 
bilateral trade, economic cooperation and investment ties. It was agreed that 
operational difficulties in the implementation of the existing Agreements would be 
reviewed and addressed in a prompt and constructive manner. The two sides agreed to 
intensify their cooperation to control unauthorised trade.

respective territories to be used for activities directed against or prejudicial to the 
security of the other. 
The two sides had a useful exchange of views on issues relating to the 
India-Nepal Treaty of Peace and Friendship as directed by the two Prime Ministers. They 
discussed various aspects of the Treaty in a candid and open manner and agreed to 
continue their discussions keeping in mind the perceptions, concerns and interests of

Suggestions to Make India More Advance in IT Sector 
777. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PR ASAD: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the President of Bell Labs, while discussing 
with the Prime Minister suggested that the country needed to bring 
communication within the reach of entire population by creating a fool- proof, 
low cost network architecture and simultaneously providing basic services, 
shared services for villages and network data communications for the software 
industry in order to enable the country to leap from other nation in IT: and 
(b) if so, the details of those suggestions and the steps being taken to 
move forward in this direction? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (SHRI PRAMOD 
MAHAJAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Details arc given in the Statement. 
128 

[ 1 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
Details of suggestions given by President of Bell Labs 
(i) The main suggestion* of President of Bell Labs are: 
* Creation of a world class tel ecommunication infrastructure by 
leveraging existing assets and new technologies. 
* Building a high capacity core network using optical switching, wave 
length division multiplexed transport and a mesh architecture. 
* Low cost high speed, optical, metro access networks. 
* Domestic Web-hosting infrastructure for local regional and international 
markets. 
* A soft switch based open communication platform for fixed and mobile 
applications. 
* Provision of low cost high speed internet access, telephony and digital 
video by exploiting the existing enteiwinment infrastructure. 
* Low cost wireless access for basic telephone services for rural villages. 
* High speed access via Communication Cafes to serve large number of 
use in rural areas. 
* Utilisation of existing infrasturcture (e.g. Re-use existing fibre for metro 
and core networks and use of existing rights of ways of railways, etc. 
* Conversion of existing GSM network to 3G/GPRS broadband systems 
(ii)      Steps being taken up in India vis-a-vis solutions suggested by 
President of Bell Labs: 
* The approach suggested by President, Bell Labs, is generally being 
followed by DOT. 
* BSNL and various private operators are laying optical fibres on a large 
scale throughout the country for establishing a broad band network. 
The present BSNL network consists of more than 2 lakh route kms of 
optical fibre cables and STM 16 systems of 2.5 Gb/s capacity for long 
distance communications. At present th e optical network is in a ring 
structure to suit the present traffic requirements. The same will be 
transformed into a Mesh network as  and when the traffic between the 
nodes justify such an arrangement. 
* India has already initiate steps to introduce WDM for transmission 
links and IP routers/ATM switches for the nodes as suggested by president 
of Bell Labs. Telecom Engineering Centre (TEC) has released 
129 

RAJYA SABHA [ 1 March, 2001 ] 
specifications for 816 wave lengt h Dense Wave Division Multiplex 
(DWDM) system which will have the capacity of 40Gbps. Trial routes 
in ring configuration have been planned using 8 window WDM in 
BSNL network. C-DOT has also taken up the development of DWDM 
based on TEC specificaitons. We have planned to deploy DWDM 
progressively in the network as capacity requirement escalates. 
* The other key technology, namely, ATM switch has been recently 
developed indigenously by C DOT. These switches are being deployed 
on a trial basis in the 4 metros and the city of Bangalore. These switches 
have 2.5 GB/s capacity. Routers are also being installed by BSNL to 
create a national internet backbone. 
* As regards the access network, fibre to the high end residential customers 
is planned to be introduced progressively either through Passive Optical 
Network (PON) or optical Digital Loop Carrier systems (DLC). 
* As a part of strategy to optimize the utilizaiton of existing copper lines 
extensive use of ADSL technology has been planned. 
* Regarding cellular, both BSNL, MTNL and private operators have 
ambitious plans to expand rapidly their GSM network. As part of 
indigenous devleopment C-DOT has upgraded its fixed line switches 
to include GSM technology. C-DOT is already developing future 
upgrades of its GSM switch include GPRS and IN services. A high level 
Focus Action Group has been set up in DOT to coordinate various 
issues related to 3 G. 
* BSNL has planned in a big way wireless in local loop (CDMA, core 
DECT, GSM and C-DOTTDMA PMP systems) for covering the villages. 
Satellite terminals to cover remote and isolated villages have also been 
planned. 
* BSNL has planned operation of cyber dhabas in all block headquarters 
(more than 6000) subject ot local entrepreneurs' readiness to set up such 
dhabas. 
* C-DOT has already developed service logic for IN services on generic 
platform. More applications on such generic platforms are being 
developed. 
* Other suggestions of President of Bell Labs like Optimal core network 
using optical switch, Lamda router, etc. are futuristic in nature and DOT 
is keeping a close watch on developments in these emerging 
technologies so that they can be introduced in India without any delay.

Functions of Controller of Certifying Authorities 
The Controller of Certifying Authorities under the Information Technology 
Act, 2000 may perform all or any of the following functions, namely:— 
1. exercising supervision over the activities of the Certifying Authorities; 
2. issue of licence to Certifying Authorities for them to issue Digital 
Signature Certificates; 
3. renewal of licence for Certifying Authority; 
4. recognition of foreign Certifying Authority; 
5. certifying public keys of the Certifying Authorities; 
6. suspension or revocation of licence to Certifying Authorities; 
7. laying down the standardsto be maintained by the Certifying Authorities; 
8. specifying the qualifications and experience which employees of the 
Certifying Authorities should possess; 
9. specifying the conditions subject to which the Certifying authorities shall 
conduct their business; 
 
10. specifying the contents of written, printed or visual materials and 
advertisements that may be distributed or used in respect of a Digital 
Signature Certificate and the public key; 
11. specifying the form and content of Digital Signature Certificate and the key; 
12. specifying the form and manner in which accounts shall be maintained by 
the Certifying Authorities; 
13. specifying the terms and conditions subject to which auditors may be 
appointed and the remuneration to be paid to them; 
14. facilitating the establishment of any electronic system by a Certifying 
Authority either solely or jointly with other Certifying Authorities and 
regulation of such systems; 
15. specifying the manner in which the Certifying Authorities shall conduct 
their dealings with the subscribers; 
16. resolving any conflict of interests between the Certifying Authorities and 
the subscribers;

17. laying down the duties of Certifying Authorities; 
18. Maintaining a data base containing the disclosure record of every 
Certifying Authority containing such particulars as may be specified by

19. Act as repository of all Digital Signature Certificates issued under 
Information Technology Act, 2000; 
20. Maintain a computerized database of al I public keys in such a manner that

National Task Force on Information Technology and Software 
Development: 
2. A High Powered National Task Force on Information Technology and 
Software Development was set up in May 1998, to formulate the draft of National 
Informatics Policy to make India an Information Technology Super Power and 
one of the largest generators and exporters of software in the world. The task 
force report aims at maki ng India a front-runner in  the age of information 
revolution as IT is perceived as an agent of transformation which will bring 
about a knowledge based society in the twenty-first century. In its first report 
the task force has made 108 recomme ndations which have been accepted by 
the Government. The Task Force has come out with Action Plan for Software 
and Hardware Development and a LongTerm National Information Technology 
Policy. 
The Task Force has, inter alia, suggested setting up a world class Info-
Infrastructure, creation of policy ambiance for the Indian IT Industry to target 
for a 50 billion U.S. $ annual export of IT software and IT services, universal 
access in internet and intranet by th e year 2008 with  IT application 
encompassing every walk of economic  and social life of the country, 
development of IT hardware industry through enabling fiscal and financial 
policies, procedural simplification, meeting working capital requirements of 
the industry, setting up venture capital fund, etc. 
The task force has estimated that IT industry is likely to generate 
employment for about 22 lakh professionals by the year 2008.

Task force on Infrastructure: 
3. The Prime Minister's Task Force on Infrastructure was set up in October 
1998 under the Chairmanship of Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission, 
comprising both Government and industry representatives, with the aim of 
attracting investment to specific projects of national and regional importance 
and ensuring their speedy completion. The task force was also required to 
formulate an Integrated National Transport policy to strengthen the transport 
infrastructure in the country and recommend steps that can significantly improve 
and foster reform in those key segments of the economy. It was also assigned 
the task of preparing a plan of action to operationalise the following decisions 
taken by the Government:—  
(i) Linking the four metros of Delhi, Mumbai, Chennas and Kolkata in the 
"Golden Quadrilateral" by four/six lane national highways as part of 
the National Highways Development Project. 
(ii) To create expressways along north-south and east-west corridors to link 
the country from north to south and east to west. 
(iii) To prepare a plan to upgrade the five international airports of Delhi, 
Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata and Bangalore to international standards. 
(iv) To convert the major ports of the country to a corporate structure and 
(v)  To prepare an integrated transport policy for the country. 
4. A draft Integrated Transport Policy has been under consideration of the 
Task Force. The recommendations on Railways, Roads, Shipping, Inland Water 
Transport and Civil Aviation in the draft Integrated transport Policy have been 
accepted by the Task Force on Infrastructure. The recommendations in regard 
to the Ports and Urban Transport sectors are proposed to be discussed in the 
meeting of the Task Force after which the Integrated Transport Policy will be 
finalised. 
5. So far, the Task Force has held 10 meetings and has submitted two 
interim reports to the Prime Minister. Among the major recommendations of the 
Task Force which have been implemented by the Government so far are: 
(i) A cess of Rs. 0.50 has been levied on the sale of every litre of diesel 
since 1st April, 1999 to raise resources for the development of roads in 
the country. Half of the collections  from this cess go toward creating 
rural roads, while the other half will be spent on development of national 
highways and State roads. 
160 

[1 March, 2001] RAJYASABHA 
(ii) The National Highways Development Project (NHDP) has been 
formulated to develop 13252 Kms. of national highways over a ten year 
period ending 2009 at a total cost of Rs. 58,000 crores. The "Golden 
Quadrilateral" portion of this project, covering the four metros, will be 
completed by 2003. 
(iii) The four metro airports of Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata will be 
offered on long term operating lease to private sector operators by the end 
of the calendar year 2000. A new international airport will be developed 
at Bangalore with private sector participation. 
(iv) A road map for the corporatisation of major ports has been finalized. 
6. Task Force on Employment Opportunities: 
In pursuance of the decision taken by the Government to the effect that ten 
crore people should get employment opportunities over the next ten years implying 
that one crore people should get employment opportunities every year, a Task 
Force on "Employment Opportunities" was set up in January 1999. The Task Force 
has, so far, conducted seven meetings and its Report is awaited.

(b) The latest estimates of State-wise  poverty available for the year

(c) There is a three-pronged action to alleviate and reduce the poverty in 
the country. These are: (i) acceleration of economic growth, (ii) human and social 
development through literacy, education, health, nutrition, meeting of the 
minimum needs, elevation of social and economic status of the weaker sections 
of the society, etc., and (iii) direct attack on poverty through employment and 
income generating programmes and assets-building for the poor. 
The increase in income of the people living below the poverty line occur 
from the joint impact of general growth process and direct income generation 
of the poor arising from various anti-poverty programmes introduced from time 
to time by the Government for their upliftment. Since the Sixth Five Year Plan 
162 

[ 1 March, 2001 ] RA JYA SABHA 
(1980-85), the Government has been implementing employment and asset 
generation schemes for the upliftment of the people living below the poverty 
line. These schemes are mainly of two types, self-employment and wage 
employment. Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) has been the 
major self-employment programme and it has been in operation in all the blocks 
of the country since 1980. The wage employment programme initially was 
National Rural Employment Programme (NREP) during the Sixth Plan period. 
In the Seventh Plan, another wage employment programme under the name 
Rural Labour Employment Guarantee Programme, (RLEGP) was introduced Then 
in 1989. Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) was launched by merging the National 
Rural Employment Programme and the Rural Labour Employment Guarantee 
Programme, and it became the main wage-employment programme. In addition, 
several programmes to help the poor were also in operation until March, 1999. 
These programmes are: Million Wells Scheme (MWS), EmploymentAssurance 
Scheme (E AS), Development ofWomen and Children in Rural Areas (DWCRA), 
Training of Rural Youth for Self-Employment (TRYSEM), Supply of Improved 
Toolkits to Rural Artisans (S1TRA). 
From 1st April, 1999, these programmes, excepting EAS and JRY have 
been restructured into single self-employment programme called the 
Swamajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with the primary objectives of 
focussed approach to poverty alleviation, capitalising advantages of group 
lending, and overcoming the problems associated with multiplicity of 
programmes. Also, from 1st April, 1999, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) has been 
restructured as Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana (JGS Y) with the primary objective 
of creation of demand driven community village infrastructure including durable 
assets at the village level and assets to enable the rural poor to increase the 
opportunities for sustained employment. Its secondary objective is generation 
of supplementary employment for the unemployed poor in the rural areas. The 
wage employment under the programme is given to Below Poverty Lines (BPL) 
families. 
From 1.12.1997, Swama Jayanti Sahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is the main 
poverty alleviation programme in the urban areas. The SJSRY, which has 
subsumed all the earlier three urban poverty alleviation programmes, viz., Nehru 
Rozgar Yojana (NRY), Urban Basic Se rvices for the Poor (UBSP), Prime 
Minister's Integrated Urban Poverty Eradication Programme (PMIUPEP), seeks 
to provide gainful employment to unemployed or underemployed urban and 
educated up to IX standard for setting up self employment ventures or provision 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [I March,2001] 
of wage employment. The implementa tion of SJSRY is relying on suitable 
community structures on the UBSP pattern and delivery of inputs under this 
programme is through the medium of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and such 
community structure.

The increase in income of the people living below the poverty line occur 
167 

RAJYASABHA [1 March,2001] 
from the joint impact of general growth process and direct income generation 
of the poor arising from various anti-poverty programmes introduced from 
time to time by the Government for their upiiftment. Since the Sixth Five 
Year Plan (1980—85), the Government has been implementing employment 
and asset generation schemes for the upiiftment of the people living below the 
poverty line. These schemes are mainly of two types, self-employment and 
wage employment. Integrated Rural Development Programme (1RDP) has 
been the major self-employment programme and it has been in operation in 
all the blocks of the country since 1980. The wage employment programme 
initially was National Rural Employment Programme (NREP) during the 
Sixth Plan period. In the Seventh Plan, another wage employment programme 
under the name Rural Labour Employment Guarantee Programme (RLEGP) 
was introduced. Then in 1989, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) was launched 
by merging the National Rural Employment Programme and the Rural Labour 
Employment Guarantee Programme, and it became the main wage-
employment programme. In addition, several programmes to help the poor 
were also in operation until March, 1999. These programmes are: Million 
Wells Scheme (MWS), Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS), Development 
of Women and Children in Rural Area (DWCRA), Training of Rural Youth 
for Self-Employment (TRYSEM), Supply of Improved Toolkits to Rural 
Artisans (SITR A). 
From 1st April, 1999, these programmes, excepting EAS and JRY have 
been restructured into single se lf-employment programme called the 
Swamajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with the primary objectives of 
focussed approach to poverty alleviation, capitalising advantages of group 
lending, and overcoming the problems associated with multiplicity of 
programmes. Also, from 1st April, 1999, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) has been 
restructured as Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana (JGS Y) with the primary objective 
of creation of demand driven community village infrastructure including durable 
assets at the village level and assets to  enable the rural poor to increase the 
opportunities for sustained employment. Its secondary objective is generation 
of supplementary employment for the unemployed poor in the rural areas. The 
wage employment under the programme is given to Below Poverty Lines (BPL) 
families. 
From 1.12.1997, Swama Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is the 
main poverty alleviation programme in the urban areas. The SJSRY, which has 
subsumed all the earlier three urban poverty alleviation programmes, viz., Nehru 
168 

[ 1 March, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
Rozgar Yojana (NRY), Urban Basic Services for the Poor (UBSP), Prime Minister's 
Integrated urban Poverty Eradication Programme (PMIUPER), seeks to provide 
gainful employment to unemployed to underemployed urban and educated up 
to IX standard for setting up self employment ventures or provision of wage 
employment. The implemenation of SJSRY is relying on suitable community 
structures on the UBSP pattern and delivery of inputs under this programme is 
through the medium of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and such community structure.

Restructuring of Planning Commission 
811. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA': Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is a proposal to review the planning system as also to 
restructure the Planning Commission; 
(b) if so, reasons therefore; and 
(c) the salient feature thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) Yes, Sir. Planning Commission is currently engaged 
in an exercise to determine what would be the most effective role for the 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [ 1 March, 2001 ] 
Commission in the altered domestic and global scenario. In this regard, a note 
prepared on the Role of the Planning Commission in the wake of changing 
economic scenario was discussed in the full Planning Commission Meeting held 
on 30th September, 2000 under the chairmanship of the Prime Minister. The 
proposal was broadly approved and is to be further discussed between the 
Deputy Chairman and the Union Finance Minister. 
(b) and (c) In the face of changing domestic economic policy regime and 
an equally fast paced integration of the economy with the emerging global order, 
investment planning is no more the only, or the more predominant, or even the 
most effective instrument of pursuing development. In fact, the role of state and 
hence of planning has to move from a direct intervention in economic activity in 
general and the production process in particular, to facilitating creation of an 
environment that encourages individual initiative and reaches out by providing 
opportunity to all. Planning has to, therefore, go beyond undertaking mere 
budgetary allocations, between the competing sectors and regions, for that 
alone would not be enough, and move towards ensuring policy harmonisation 
over time and across space. This requires the Planning Commission to strengthen its 
role as a Think Tank'—a repository of expert knowledge.

835. SHRI S. AGNIRAJ: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) what steps are being taken to give protection to the SSI units in view 
of ongoing liberalisation process; 
(b) whether it is also a fact th at many MNCs are coming up in 
manufacturing items reserved for SSIs;

(d) whether it is also a fact that investment limit in SSI is being raised and if 
so, by when it is coming into force? 
189 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI 
VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) In view of the increase in competition anticipated 
due to the removal of Quantitative Restrictions (QRs), the Government recently 
announced a comprehensive policy package to strengthen the small scale sector 
and enhance its competitiveness both domestically and globally. The policy 
package includes easier access to credit, availability of collateral free composite 
loans upto Rs. 25 lakhs, capital subs idy for technological upgradation and 
improved infrastructure.

knitwear and handtools industries, raising the investment limit to Rs. 5 crores, has

period specified in the Industries (Development & Regulation) Act, 1951.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRIARUN SHOURIE): (a) Member of 
Parliament are approached by their constituents, quite often, for small works of 
capital nature to be done in their constituencies. There was a demand from MPs 
that they should be able to recommend works to be done in their constituencies. 
Considering these suggestions, the Prime Minister announced in the Parliament 
on 23rd December, 1993 the MP Local Area Development Scheme. 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [ 1 March, 2001 ] 
Under the Scheme, each MP will have a choice to suggest to the Head of 
the District works which are developmental in nature, leading to creation of 
durable assets, based on locally felt need s, to the tune of Rs. 2 crore per year 
which can be taken up in his/her constituency. Elected Members of Rajya 
Sabha representing the whole of the Stat e as they do, may select works for 
implementation in one or more distri cts as they may choose. Nominated 
Members of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha may also select-works for 
implementation in one or more Districts anywhere in the country. 
(b) and (c) A number of requests from the Members of Parliament were 
received suggesting that in view of unprecedented calamit y in Gujarat, a 
relaxation in Guidelines on MPLADS be made to allow MPs to contribute 
whatever they can from their MPLADS  fund towards the rebuilding of the 
affected areas. Accordingly, the provis ions contained in para 1-.3 of the 
Guidelines were relaxed allowing MPs to contribute any amount they desire 
from their MPLADS funds subject to their annual entitlement for taking up 
developmental works that arejiermissible in the Guidelines fortehabilitation 
in the earthquake affected areas of Gujarat.

843. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the PRIME MINISTER

(a) whether it is a fact that there has been no change in the Socio-economic

in KBK (Kalahandi, Bolangir, Koraput) districts, there had been no visible

A RUN SHOURIE): (a) Yes, Sir. The socio-economic condition of Bolangir

implementation of schemes, besides certain policies followed by the State 
Government are among the reasons for the slow socio- economic development 
of the KBK region. 
(d) Efforts are being made to mitigate the endemic poverty of this region 
through a three pronged approach: (i) Drought—proofing through watershed 
development, afforestation and extension of irrigation facilities; (ii) A more 
responsive administration; and (iii) A change in some of the policies of the 
State Government related to non-timber forest produce, land acquisition, 
restoration of alienated land and autonomy to village panchayats in financial 
matters.

SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI (Uttar Pradesh): Mr. Chairman, Sir,

[1 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, I deem it a matter of honour to move this 
Motion of Thanks. I believe that the Address, delivered by the hon. 
President, has helped in removing a lot of cobwebs on many of the 
issues, policies and programmes. In view of the fact that the country 
has undergone a number of transform ations during the last decade 
and many of the issues getting more and more complicated -- 
somehow or other, not always comprehendable - the Address that he 
has delivered to the joint session takes into account the radical 
transformations in various fields and the changes that have taken 
place in the social, political, international, economic, scientific and 
educational areas. As they impinge on our country, he has really taken 
a synoptic view of these changes , events, initiatives and also 
perceptions for the future and imperat ives of today, so that we can 
have a better, comprehensive, vision as well as an agenda for action. 
Sir, when the problems are numerous and complex, and 
relate to a country of our vastness, the elucidation of the rationale of 
these issues is bound to be more elaborate. The hon. President has 
really thrown open the windows for us to comprehend them. He has 
touched the essentials and the fu ndamentals, the core and the 
substantive issues, and not just airy nothings. He has provided us 
luminosity so that we can comprehend the place our country has, in 
the third millennium, in this global world, the potential it has and the 
path that it has to take for the flowering of that potential and the 
fulfilment of its genius, or, what Shri Nehru called, "the tryst with 
destiny." 
Sir, the President's Address begins by referring to the 
unfortunate devastation, the great tragedy, that overtook; the 
earthquake in Gujarat. He spoke really for the entire nation in this hour 
of solemn grief. The House discussed it  at some length, with a lot of 
understanding and with an immense seriousness of purpose. Our 
hearts go in sympathy and support to the afflicted p eople of Gujarat. 
Sir, he referred to the coordinated effort and the coordinated response 
of both the State Governments and the Government of India. He 
expressed the nation's gratefulness to the humanitarian aid received 
from various countries and agencies abroad. He also expressed his 
appreciation for the tremendous, really stupendous, service rendered 
by the Armed Forces of our country. He also expressed his praise and 
appreciation for the yeoman's service which was done, and for the 
relief and rescue work which was undertaken by the voluntary groups, 
NGOs, many philanthropic organisations and social service 
organisations. Sir, all of us are aware that in 
201 

RAJYA SABHA         [1 March, 2001] 
rendering relief and rehabilitation, the people and the various agencies 
were motivated truly by humanitarian considerations- There was no 
discrimination on any ground, whethe r sectarian or otherwise, in 
providing relief to the people, and this shows the unity of purpose and 
also the unity of heart that the people of this country have. 
But, Sir, as he very rightly pointed out, there is a need to learn 
lessons from the catastrophe which overtook Gujarat, the super-
cyclone which was there in Orissa, and from the floods and drought in 
other parts of the country; and that is , what I think, is most important 
for us today. The need is to set, modernise, expand and strengthen 
the management capabilities and,  if possible, anticipate these 
catastrophes in advance. That is why, Sir* the first thing, the important 
thing is the need for updating the rules and regulations that govern 
building construction, town planning, etc. A number of suggestions 
were made by the hon. Members in this regard, and the hon. Minister, 
Shri Jagmohan, the other day, mentioned what was being done and 
what has been done. The need really is to enforce those rules and 
regulations. 
Sir, here, I think, is the opportunity where no quarter be given 
not only to those who are responsible for the lapses and inadequacies 
that led to the tragedy and to t he delays. The tragedy was a natural 
calamity. But why did the buildings fall? What was the kind of nexus? I 
think it is here that the Government should take the most ruthless 
action so that it is a lesson for the people. I think, Sir, this is also an 
opportunity when this nexus of Mafiosi, the nexus among the 
construction people, the building people the engineers, the contractors 
etc. is broken. 
I think, from Gujarat, we shou ld take a lesson for the entire 
country. For Gujarat, of course, we prav along with the hon. President 
that the quality of the life of t he people after this tragedy should be a 
better one. 
Sir, he emphasised on a comprehensive disaster 
management plan at the Centre and in the States. We have some 
scattered plans of a routine type. Un fortunately, in many of the States, 
we have not revised them even in a ro utine way, as is called tor. This 
is where only a ritualistic approach , unfortunately, prevails in the 
administration. Now, here is t he time to have a comprehensive 
management plan on a much larger scale. It should be formulated in 
consultation with the States.   I think this is the priority.   It is

[1 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
here that all the talents in this count ry, whether they are in the field of 
construction or institutions, of engineering, architecture or other scientific

President, it is not a criticism of the President of the Republic, but it is a 
criticism of the Government of the day. Sir, the President, in his Address, 
covering 69 paragraphs, has devoted a substantial part of the Address 
to the state of the economy, paragraphs 9 to 46, to which I will come a

in the President's Address. No doubt, administration came up to the 
mark, and dealing with a congregation of such a vast multitude of 
people at a given point of time requires a lot of administrative sk ill, but,

Sir, while talking about the internal security which has been 
dealt with in paragraphs 11 to 15, I would like to discuss it in a little 
detail, because both the Mover of  the Motion and the Seconder have 
dealt with it at length. No doubt,- the initiatives which have been taken 
in Kashmir have received the endors ement of a cross-section of the 
people. No doubt, there has been relative peace in the North-Eastern 
States. But, two major points emerge in regard to internal security. As 
the President in his Address has also referred to stepping up the 
financial assistance from the Centre to the States for modernisation of 
the police forces, certain policy matters  arise. First of all, as per the 
scheme of the Constitution of our country, maintenance of public order 
and enforcement of law are the mo st crucial powers which have been 
vested the State Governments. But, in recent years, we find that 
whenever there is a disturbance in respect of public order, or, 
sometimes even for normal election duty which should be taken care 
of by the State Governments, the Central paramilitary forces are 
requisitioned. 
Why is it happening? Is the law enforcing machinery in the 
States inadequate? If it is inadequate,  instead of distorting the federal 
structure, which is the scheme of  the Constitution, why can't you 
strengthen the law enforcing machinery of the state? That is why it is a 
welcome moveT In fact, the Parliamentary Standing Committee, which 
I am heading.had dealt with this matter and had subsequently 
recommended that the police force in the States must be modernised 
and the CBI, the Central investi gating agency, should not undertake 
the normal investigation duties and other duties which are assigned to 
the State Police. The maintena nce of law and order is the 
responsibility of the State admin istration, and, for that, frequent 
requisitioning of the Central Paramilitary Forces is not correct. A 
serious distortion has occurred here. Certain forces were created, built 
up and trained. A lot of investment has taken place to acquire 
specialised skills. Take the IT BP. Take the BSF. The ITBP was 
created to have combating skills in high altitudes, in mountainous 
terrain. Now, if the ITBP is utilised to protect the personal safety and 
security of some personalities or for certain other work, the whole 
purpose of raising the Force is defeated. Similarly, the BSF should 
develop expertise on preventing smu ggling and preventing infiltration 
along the border areas. If you deploy them frequently just to help the 
State administration, to maintain normal law and order situations in the 
States, then, we would not get the best of the service from them. 
Moreover, we are receiving constant  complaints about the CRPF, the 
BSF and the ITBP. It is complained that they are put under so much 
sress and strain that their

SHRI V.P. DURAISAMY (Tamil Nadu): Madam, very aptly, the 
President has devoted five paragraphs to Gujarat and the devastation 
caused to it by the earthquake. We  are very sad that thousands of 
lives have been lost. Public and priv ate property worth thousands of 
crores were destroyed. The entire nation heeded the call given by the 
hon. Prime Minister to provide financial and material help to our 
brothers and sisters in Gujarat. According to the latest Press report, 
more than Rs.2,000 crores have been contributed from the Prime 
Minister's Relief Fund. I am glad, the NDA Government is going to set 
up a permanent Disaster Management Authority. The Government has 
also requested HUDCO to issue Rs .1,500 crores worth of tax-free-
bonds. I would request my friends in the Opposition not to the 
politicise this issue relating to the relief and rehabilitation work in 
Gujarat. We all know that they are bringing the issue of discrimination, 
with an eye on the coming elections. 
We all agree that we have social and economic inequality. 
We, the politicians, should make every effort to make our country a 
land of justice and equal opportunity for our citizens. 
Madam, para 9 deals with participation of women in the 
political process, not only as voters but also as elected representatives 
and holders of executive responsibility. We are all aware of the under-
representation of our sisters in Parliament and State Legislatures. I 
congratulate the NDA Government for introducing the Constitution 
(Eighty-Fifth) Amendment Bill in 1999 in the Lok Sabha. But some 
political parties are not in favour of  the Bill and they are obstructing it 
from being passed. Our party, the DMK, is for women's empowerment.    
The Tamil Nadu Government has already
